nodes.content: Design a tiered MVCC storage engine preserving snapshot isolation and safe reclamation during concurrent migration, writes, and crashes.
requirements: Acknowledged writes and snapshot-required versions survive crashes at every migration and reclamation transition.
Migration increases p99 read latency by at most 20% versus identical workloads without migration.

nodes.content: Use WAL-first MVCC writes, fsynced copy-on-write migration manifests, durable snapshot pins, epoch-gated reclamation, and read-priority copying.
How can tier relocation survive crashes without losing concurrent WAL-committed writes or versions pinned by active snapshots?
After destination fsync, durable WAL replay fences, and pin persistence, manifest swaps yield zero lost acknowledged or snapshot-visible versions.
Run CrashMatrix-1 with concurrent writes and pinned snapshots; crash at copy/fsync/swap/reclaim barriers and verify recovered versions against an oracle.
CrashMatrix-1: 40,000 crashes across four barriers yielded zero missing acknowledged writes or snapshot-visible versions versus the recovery oracle.
Adopt WAL-fenced, fsynced manifest swaps and durable snapshot pins with epoch reclamation; gate rollout on p99 latency.
After adopting crash-safe swaps, benchmark identical migrating and control workloads in TierBench-1; tune copy throttling for p99 ratio ≤1.20.
Run TierBench-1 with 32 clients and 100-GiB data, measuring migrating/control read-p99 ratios across 16–128 MiB/s copy-rate caps.
TierBench-1 report containing read-p99 migrating/control ratios by copy-rate cap, throughput, and workload configuration.
Analyze TierBench-1 report to find the highest copy-rate cap meeting read-p99 ratio ≤1.20 across tested configurations.
TierBench-1: read-priority copying at 64 MiB/s held worst-case migrating/control read-p99 ratio at 1.17; 128 MiB/s reached 1.26.
When can source extents and superseded versions be reclaimed while readers hold old manifest epochs or snapshots remain pinned?
Implement ReclaimGuard: after durable manifest detachment, drain reader epochs, check persisted snapshot pins, then journal and delete eligible extents.
ReclaimGuard fault tests: 10,000 reader/pin interleavings with 5,000 crash injections showed zero premature source deletes or missing pinned versions.
Run HoldDrain-1 with hour-long pre-swap readers and snapshots; confirm reclamation blocks until both release, then frees extents after restart.
HoldDrain-1: a persisted pin expired after 60 minutes; post-restart ReclaimGuard deleted 12 source extents before snapshot release.
How can durable snapshot pins protect long-lived snapshots across restarts without lease expiry triggering premature reclamation?
Nonexpiring, fsynced snapshot pins retained until explicit durable release prevent premature deletion across crashes and hour-long snapshots.
Use n13’s zero-loss baseline to assess regression; replay n15’s expiry failure with fsynced nonexpiring pins at n10’s 64 MiB/s cap.
HoldDrain-2: 10,000 crash/restart interleavings with two-hour snapshots showed zero premature deletions; all 12 extents reclaimed after durable release.
Run PinBarrier-1: crash around pin-create and release fsync during migration; verify surviving snapshots and eventual post-release reclamation.
PinBarrier-1: 4/20,000 post-fsync crashes restored stale pin checkpoints, dropping unreleased pins and prematurely reclaiming snapshot versions.
Can read-priority copying keep the migrating/control read-p99 ratio ≤1.20 during bursty read traffic?
Repair stale-checkpoint pin replay, repeat two-hour snapshot checks, then measure burst-read p99 ratio at 64 MiB/s against controls.
After pin-replay repair, two-hour snapshots survived 20,000 crashes; BurstRead-1 at 64 MiB/s yielded a read-p99 ratio of 1.24.
Reject fixed 64 MiB/s copying for bursty reads; throttle migration adaptively when read-p99 ratio approaches 1.20.
Implement queue-depth-triggered copy throttling from 64 to 16 MiB/s, then rerun BurstRead-1 against identical unmigrated controls.
Implement 8-request queue-depth throttling to 16 MiB/s; rerun BurstRead-1 and compare read-p99 against unmigrated controls.
BurstRead-2 report with 8-request throttling configuration, migrating/control read-p99 ratios, and copy-throughput traces.
Use a unified replay-sequenced journal for MVCC writes, snapshot pins, and extent retirement, with generation-fenced dual reads and adaptive copying.
How should checkpoint recovery order pin creation, MVCC commits, and extent retirement to prevent stale replay from dropping snapshot versions?
Atomically checkpoint journal high-watermarks; replay later records in sequence and revalidate retirements against recovered pins before deleting extents.
Run ReplayOrder-1 with 50,000 crashes at checkpoint, pin, commit, and retirement barriers; compare recovered versions to an MVCC oracle.
ReplayOrder-1: 50,000 injected crashes produced zero missing acknowledged commits or pinned versions; deferred retirements replayed safely.
After ReplayOrder-1, stress generation-fenced dual reads and adaptive copying with concurrent snapshots, writes, crashes; measure version loss and read-p99.
GenBurst-1: adaptive copying and generation-fenced dual reads preserved all versions but raised worst-case migrating/control read-p99 ratio to 1.23.
Retain replay-sequenced commit/pin/retirement journaling; replace dual reads with epoch-protected single-hop pointers and preempt copies when reads queue.
Implement epoch-protected single-hop reads and preemptible copying; rerun ReplayOrder-1 and GenBurst-1, requiring zero lost versions and read-p99 ratio ≤1.20.
Implement epoch-pinned single-hop pointers with atomic publication and queue-triggered copy preemption; rerun ReplayOrder-1 and GenBurst-1.
TierMVCC-v3 patchset with epoch-pinned single-hop pointers, atomic publication, preemptible copying, and ReplayOrder-1/GenBurst-1 regression logs.
Audit TierMVCC-v3 logs; independently rerun 50,000 crash injections and GenBurst-1, checking lost versions and read-p99 ratio ≤1.20.
TierMVCC-v3: 50,000 crashes lost zero acknowledged writes or pinned versions; GenBurst-1 worst-case migrating/control read-p99 ratio was 1.16.
Can queue-triggered copy preemption finish migration under sustained read pressure while keeping the read-p99 ratio ≤1.20?
Run SustainRead-1 on TierMVCC-v3 with 32 sustained readers; measure 100-GiB migration completion and read-p99 versus identical unmigrated controls.
SustainRead-1: despite copy preemption, migrating/control read-p99 reached 1.27, and the 100-GiB migration copied only 7 GiB in 24 hours.
How do epoch-pinned single-hop reads remain safe when migration publishes a new pointer while old source extents await reclamation?
Extend TierMVCC-v3 crash tests with SustainRead-1 readers; pause at pointer publication, crash, and verify reads and source retention.
PointerPause-1: 30,000 publication/crash schedules showed zero dangling reads; source extents remained until old reader epochs drained.
Retain epoch-pinned single-hop publication for safety; revise copy scheduling separately because sustained reads violate latency and progress targets.
Preserve epoch-before-pointer-load and durable publication; verify source retirement waits for old reader epochs after scheduling changes using PointerPause-1.
Add 16-KiB copy quanta with per-shard minimum bandwidth; rerun PointerPause-1 and verify retired extents remain until reader epochs drain.
TierMVCC-v3.1 patchset adding 16-KiB copy quanta and per-shard bandwidth floors, with PointerPause-1 retirement-safety logs.
Isolate TierMVCC-v3.1’s 16-KiB copy quanta and per-shard floors on dedicated migration queues, retaining journaled pins and epoch-safe reclamation.
Can dedicated migration queues maintain sustained migration progress without exceeding a 1.20 migrating/control read-p99 ratio?
Dedicated migration queues with 16-KiB copy quanta sustain ≥8 GiB/h under 32 readers while keeping read-p99 ratio ≤1.20.
Run SustainRead-2 with 32 readers and a 100-GiB migration, measuring hourly copy throughput and migrating/control read-p99 ratio.
SustainRead-2: migration sustained 9.1 GiB/h, but shared-device contention raised the migrating/control read-p99 ratio to 1.22.
Run SustainRead-3, sweeping dedicated migration queue depth 1–4; check hourly throughput ≥8 GiB/h and read-p99 ratio ≤1.20.
SustainRead-3: queue depth 1 sustained 8.3 GiB/h with a migrating/control read-p99 ratio of 1.18.
Does queue-depth-one migration preserve acknowledged writes and snapshot-pinned versions when crashes interrupt source retirement?
After SustainRead-2’s latency failure and SustainRead-3’s queue-depth-one pass, inject 50,000 retirement crashes; verify committed writes and pinned versions.
RetireCrash-1: 50,000 queue-depth-one retirement crashes lost zero acknowledged writes or pinned versions; all eligible extents reclaimed after restart.
Adopt queue-depth-one migration with journaled retirement: RetireCrash-1 found zero losses, and SustainRead-3 met latency and progress targets.
Integrate queue-depth-one copying into release candidate; rerun RetireCrash-1 and long-lived snapshot recovery before enabling source deletion.
Build TierMVCC-rc1 with queue-depth-one copying; rerun 50,000 RetireCrash-1 injections and two-hour snapshot recovery before deletion.
TierMVCC-rc1 package with queue-depth-one migration, replay-sequenced journal, epoch-safe pointers, and RetireCrash-1/snapshot-recovery logs.
Use immutable MVCC runs, replay-sequenced pin journaling, fsynced manifest generations, and device-level read-reserved migration credits.
Prototype immutable-run migration with fsynced manifest generations and read-reserved device credits; compare against TierMVCC-rc1 in crash and p99 benchmarks.
Using BurstRead-2 traces and TierMVCC-v3.1 copy quanta, prototype fsynced immutable-run migration with read-reserved credits; benchmark against TierMVCC-rc1.
ImmutableRun-v1 prototype with fsynced manifest generations, read-reserved migration credits, and comparison logs against TierMVCC-rc1.
Evaluate ImmutableRun-v1 against TierMVCC-rc1 under SustainRead-3 and 50,000 crash injections, measuring read-p99 ratios and recovered versions.
ImmutableRun-v1: 50,000 crashes lost zero versions; SustainRead-3 read-p99 ratio was 1.14 versus TierMVCC-rc1’s 1.18.
Can read-reserved credits maintain a ≤1.20 read-p99 ratio during sustained device saturation without stalling immutable-run migration?
Reserving 80% of device IOPS for reads keeps read-p99 ratio ≤1.20 while immutable-run copying sustains ≥8 GiB/h.
Using ImmutableRun-v1’s 1.14 baseline and GenBurst-1’s 1.23 failure, saturate the device with 80% read reservation; measure p99 and GiB/h.
SaturateRead-1: 80% read reservation held read-p99 ratio at 1.15, but immutable-run migration achieved only 5.6 GiB/h.
Retain ImmutableRun-v1’s latency advantage; reject fixed 80% read reservation because saturation cuts migration below 8 GiB/h.
Replace fixed 80% read reservation with p99-guided 50–80% credits; retest saturation for ≤1.20 p99 ratio, ≥8 GiB/h, and crash safety.
Modify ImmutableRun-v1 to adjust read credits between 50–80% using 10-second p99 feedback; rerun SaturateRead-1 and retirement crashes.
ImmutableRun-v2 replaces v1’s fixed read credits with 10-second p99-guided 50–80% reservations and includes saturation/crash logs.
